{{smaller block|<poem>''Val.'' And ''on'' a love-book pray for my success.
''Pro.'' ''Upon'' some book I love I’ll pray for thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 20.}}
<poem>My saucy bark, inferior far to his,
''On'' your broad main doth wilfully appear:
Your shallowest help will hold me up afloat,
Whilst he ''upon'' your soundless deep doth ride.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxx.}}
<poem>''Upon'' the head of all who sat beneath . . .
Samson, with these immix’d, inevitably
Pull’d down the same destruction ''on'' himself.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1652.}}
<poem>The tide is full, the moon lies fair
''Upon'' the straits; —''on'' the French coast the light
Gleams and is gone. {{right|''M. Arnold'', Dover Beach.}}</poem>}}
'''To beat†, blow, fall, pass,''' etc., '''upon.''' See the verbs. —'''Upon an average, a thought, occasion, one’s hands, one’s oath,''' etc. See the nouns.

'''II.†''' ''adv.'' Hereupon; thereupon; onward; on.
{{smaller block|<poem>Til May it wol suffice ''uppon'' to fede,
But lenger not thenne Marche if it shal sede.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 181.}}
<poem>It is great morning, and the hour prefix’d
Of her delivery to this valiant Greek
Comes fast ''upon''. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 3. 3.}}</poem>}}

'''uponon†, upon­one†''', ''adv.'' At once; anon. See ''anon'' (the same word without the element ''up'').
{{smaller block|<poem>When mercury hade menyt this mater to ende,
And graunt me thise gyftis hit gladit my hert.
I onswaret hym esely euyn ''vponon''.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2418.}}}}

readings.c3s3:
¶
'''up-plight†''', ''v. t.'' [ME., < ''up'' + ''plight''<sup>3</sup>.] To fold up; carry off.
{{smaller block|The gates of the toun he hath ''upplyght.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 59.}}}}

'''up-plow''' (up-plou′), ''v. t.'' To plow up; tear up as by plowing. ''G. Fletcher.'' [Rare.]

'''up-pluck''' (up-pluk′), ''v. t.'' To pluck up; pull up. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And you, sweet flow’rs, that in this garden grow, . . .
Yourselves ''uppluck’d'' would to his funeral hie.</poem>
{{right|''G. Fletcher'', Christ’s Triumph over Death.}}}}

'''up-pricked''' (up-prikt′), ''a.'' Set up sharply or pointedly; erected; pricked up. ''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 271. [Rare.]

'''up-prop''' (up-prop′), ''v. t.'' To prop up; sustain by a prop. ''Donne'', Progress of the Soul, i.

'''up-putting''' (up′pu̇t″ing), ''n.'' Lodging; entertainment for man and beast. ''Scott.'' [Scotch.]

'''upraise''' (up-rāz′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''upreysen''; < ''up'' + ''raise''<sup>1</sup>.] To raise; lift up.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon a night
Whan that the mone ''upreysed'' had her light.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1163.}}
<poem>The man
His spear had reached in strong arms he ''upraised.''</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 323.}}}}

'''upraising''' (up′rā″zing), ''n.'' Rearing; nurture. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There was nothing of the Corydon about Hunt or his ''upraising'', as the Scotch call it.
{{right|''The Portfolio'', N. S., No. 13, p. 10.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|uplift|6661|upraising}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|There has been a wonderful ''uplift'' in the enthusiasm and faith of Christians.
{{right|''The Congregationalist'', Nov. 19, 1879.}}}}

'''uplock†''' (up-lok′), ''v. t.'' To lock up.
{{smaller block|His sweet ''up-locked'' treasure. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lii.}}}}

'''uplook''' (up-lu̇k′), ''v. i.'' To look up.

'''uplooking''' (up′lu̇k″ing), ''a.'' Looking up; aspiring.
{{smaller block|It takes stalwart and ''uplooking'' faith to make history [such as the Puritans made]. {{right|''Phelps'', My Study, p. 294.}}}}

'''uplying''' (up′lī″ing), ''a.'' Elevated; of land, upland.
{{smaller block|In ''up-lying'' situations, where the drift consists of raw material, fluxion-structures are seldom detected.
{{right|''Nature'', XXX. 530.}}}}

'''upmaking''' (up′mā″king), ''n.'' In ''ship-building'', pieces of plank or timber piled one on another as a filling up, especially those placed between the bilgeways and a ship’s bottom preparatory to launching.

'''upmost''' (up′mōst), ''a. superl.'' [< ''up'' + ''-most.'' Cf. ''uppermost.''] Highest; topmost; uppermost.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lowliness is young ambition’s ladder,
Whereto the climber-upward turns his face;
But when he once attains the ''upmost'' round,
He then unto the ladder turns his back.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 24.}}}}

'''upon''' (u-pon′), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [< ME. ''upon'', ''uppon'', ''upone'', ''opon'', ''oppon'', ''apon'', ''appone'', ''uppen'', < AS. ''uppon'', ''uppan'' (= Icel. ''up á'', ''upp á'' = Sw. ''på'' (< ''uppå'') = Dan. ''paa'', upon), upon, up on, < ''up'', ''upp'', up, + ''an'', ''on'', on: see ''up'' and ''on''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. AS. ''uppan'' (= OS. ''uppan'' = OFries. ''uppa'', ''oppa'' = OHG. ''ūfen'', ''uffen''), up, < ''up'', ''upp'' + adv. suffix ''-an'': see ''up'', ''adv.''] '''I.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' Up and on: in many cases scarcely more than a synonym of ''on'', the force of ''up'' being almost or entirely lost. See ''on''<sup>1</sup>, ''prep.'' {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Aloft on; in an elevated position on; on a high or the highest part of: noting rest or location.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The hyȝe trone ther moȝt ȝe hede . . .
The hyȝe godez self hit set ''vpone.''</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 1053.}}
<poem>Two theues also tholed deth that tyme,
''Vppon'' a crosse bisydes Cryst, so was the comune lawe.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xviii. 71.}}
<poem>We’ll have thee, as our rarer monsters are,
Painted ''upon'' a pole, and underwrit,
“Here may you see the tyrant.”</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7. 26.}}
<poem>O Angels, clap your wings ''upon'' the skyes,
And giue this Virgin Christall plaudities.</poem>
{{right|''C. Tourneur'', Revenger’s Tragedy, ii. 1.}}
<poem>Four brave Southron foragers
Stood hie ''upon'' the gait.</poem>
{{right|''Sir William Wallace'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 238).}}
<poem>Three years I lived ''upon'' a pillar, high
Six cubits, and three years on one of twelve.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', St. Simeon Stylites.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Upward so as to get or be on: involving motion toward a higher point.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The nihtegale i-h[e]rde this,
And hupte [hopped] ''uppon'' on blowe ris [branch].</poem>
{{right|''Owl and Nightingale'', l. 1636.}}}}

{{smaller block|And he xal make hym to wryte, and than gon ''upon'' a leddere, and settyn the tabyl abovyn Crystes hed.
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 324.}}}}

{{smaller block|They shall climb up ''upon'' the houses. {{right|Joel ii. 9.}}}}

<poem>Four nimble gnats the horses were, . . .
Fly Cranion the charioteer
''Upon'' the coach-box getting.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}

{{smaller block|Lucan vaulted ''upon'' Pegasus with all the heat and intrepidity of youth. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}

<poem>To lift the woman’s fall’n divinity
''Upon'' an even pedestal with man.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iii.}}}}

'''2.''' On, in any sense: conveying no notion of height, elevation, rise, or ascent. See ''on''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Aside from the uses noted in the foregoing definition, ''upon'' is strictly synonymous with ''on'', and is preferred in certain cases only for euphonic or metrical reasons. For parallel uses of the two words, see the following quotations.}}

<poem>Dere dyn ''vp-on'' day, daunsyng ''on'' nyȝtes,
Al watz hap ''vpon'' heȝe in halles & chambrez.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 47.}}}}

<poem>Swyerez [squires] that swyftly swyed ''on'' blonkez [horses],
& also fele ''vpon'' fote, of fre & of bonde.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 88.}}}}

<poem>The flode with a felle cours flowet ''on'' hepis,
Rose ''vppon'' rockes [''i. e.'', in towering masses] as any ranke hylles.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1991.}}}}

{{smaller block|Also, that euery brother and suster schul be boxom, and come whan they be warned, . . . ''vpon'' the oth th<sup>t</sup> they haue maad, and ''on'' the peyne of xl. d. to paie to the box; . . . ''Vpon'' the peyne afore-seid, but he haue a verrey enchesoun wherfore th<sup>t</sup> they mowe be excused.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 10.}}}}

<poem>That Peter’s heirs should tread ''on'' Emperors,
And walk ''upon'' the dreadful adder’s back.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marlowe'', Faustus, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Upon'' whom doth not his light arise? [Compare Mat. v. 45: He maketh his sun to rise ''on'' the evil and ''on'' the good.]
{{right|Job xxv. 3.}} <poem>''Val.'' And ''on'' a love-book pray for my success.
''Pro.'' ''Upon'' some book I love I’ll pray for thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 20.}}
<poem>My saucy bark, inferior far to his,
''On'' your broad main doth wilfully appear:
Your shallowest help will hold me up afloat,
Whilst he ''upon'' your soundless deep doth ride.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxx.}}
<poem>''Upon'' the head of all who sat beneath . . .
Samson, with these immix’d, inevitably
Pull’d down the same destruction ''on'' himself.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1652.}}
<poem>The tide is full, the moon lies fair
''Upon'' the straits; —''on'' the French coast the light
Gleams and is gone. {{right|''M. Arnold'', Dover Beach.}}</poem>}}
'''To beat†, blow, fall, pass,''' etc., '''upon.''' See the verbs. —'''Upon an average, a thought, occasion, one’s hands, one’s oath,''' etc. See the nouns.

'''II.†''' ''adv.'' Hereupon; thereupon; onward; on.
{{smaller block|<poem>Til May it wol suffice ''uppon'' to fede,
But lenger not thenne Marche if it shal sede.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 181.}}
<poem>It is great morning, and the hour prefix’d
Of her delivery to this valiant Greek
Comes fast ''upon''. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 3. 3.}}</poem>}}

'''uponon†, upon­one†''', ''adv.'' At once; anon. See ''anon'' (the same word without the element ''up'').
{{smaller block|<poem>When mercury hade menyt this mater to ende,

I onswaret hym esely euyn ''vponon''.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2418.}}}}

'''up-peak''' (up-pēk′), ''v. i.'' To rise in or to a peak. ''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iii. 209. [Rare.]

'''upper''' (up′ėr), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''upper'' (= D. ''opper'' = MLG. ''uppere''), compar. of ''up:'' see ''up'', and cf. ''over''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Higher in place: opposed to ''nether:'' as, the ''upper'' lip; the ''upper'' side of a thing; an ''upper'' story; the ''upper'' deck.
{{smaller block|<poem>And such a yell was there,
Of sudden and portentous birth,
As if men fought upon the earth,
And fiends in ''upper'' air.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, vi. 25.}}}}
'''2.''' Superior in rank or dignity: as, the ''upper'' house of a legislature; an ''upper'' servant.
{{smaller block|Few of the ''upper'' Planters drinke any water: but the better sort are well furnished with Sacke, Aquavitæ, and good English Beere.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' True Travels, II. 258.}}
Betting proper was not so much diffused through all ranks and classes [in 1845], but was more confined to the ''upper'' circles of society. ''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 842.}}
'''To have''' {{smaller|or}} '''get the upper hand.''' {{smaller|See ''hand''.}}—'''To have the upper fortune†''', {{smaller|to have the upper hand.}}
{{smaller block|You ''have the upper fortune'' of him.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune, i. 2.}}}}
'''To hold the upper hand†.''' {{smaller|Same as ''to have the upper hand''.}}—'''To keep a stiff upper lip.''' {{smaller|See ''lip''.}}—'''Upper Bench,''' {{smaller|in ''Eng. hist.'', the name given to the Court of King’s Bench during the exile of Charles II.}}—'''Upper case.''' {{smaller|See ''case''<sup>2</sup>, 6.}}—'''Upper coverts,''' {{smaller|in ''ornith.'', the coverts on the upper side of the wings and tail; superior tectrices. See ''covert'', ''n.'', 6.}}—'''Upper crust,''' {{smaller|the higher circles of society; the aristocracy; the upper ten. [Slang.]}}—'''Upper culmination.''' {{smaller|See ''culmination''.}}—'''Upper house.''' {{smaller|See ''house''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Upper keyboard.''' {{smaller|See ''keyboard''.}}—'''Upper leather.''' {{smaller|(''a'') Leather used in making the vamps and quarters of boots and shoes. (''b'') Vamps and quarters of boots and shoes collectively. Also called simply ''uppers''. Their Tables were so very Neat, and Shin’d with Rubbing, like the ''Upper Leathers'' of an Alderman’s shoes.
{{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, [I. 227.}}}}

'''Upper story,''' a story above the ground floor; the top story; hence, colloquially, the head; the brain.

{{smaller block|It knocked everything topsy-turvy in my ''upper story'', and there is some folks as says I hain’t never got right up thar sence.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXX. 348.}}}}

'''Upper ten thousand,''' or elliptically '''upper ten,''' the wealthier or more aristocratic persons of a large community; the higher circles or leading classes in society.

{{smaller block|At present there is no distinction among the ''upper ten thousand'' of the city.
{{right|''N. P. Willis'', Ephemera.}}
Here in the afternoon hours of spring and autumn is the favorite promenade of the ''upper ten.''
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVIII. 568.}}}}

'''Upper works''' (''naut.''). Same as ''dead-works.''

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The upper part of a shoe or boot, comprising the vamp and quarters.

{{smaller block|Ladies’ straight top button ''upper'' with straight toe cap.
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 109.}}}}

'''2.''' ''pl.'' Separate cloth gaiters to button above the shoes over the ankle.—'''To be on one’s uppers,''' {{smaller|to be poor or in hard luck: referring to a worn-out condition of one’s shoes. [Slang.]}}

'''upper†''' (up′ėr), ''adv. compar.'' [< ME. ''upper''; compar. of ''up'', ''adv.''] Higher.

<poem>And with this word ''upper'' to sore
He gan. ''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 884.</poem>

'''upperest†''' (up′ėr-est), ''a. superl.'' [ME. ''uppereste''; < ''upper'' + ''-est.''] Highest.

{{smaller block|By whiche degrees men myhten clymben fro the nethereste lettre to the ''uppereste.'' ''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 1.}}

'''upper-growth''' (up′ėr-grōth), ''n.'' That part of a plant or shrub which is above the ground.

{{smaller block|Here, too, was planted that strange and interesting denizen of the wilderness, the Saxaous, . . . which with a scanty and often ragged ''upper-growth'' strikes its sturdy roots deep down into the sand. {{right|''Nature'', XXXIX. 470.}}}}

'''upper-machine''' (up′ėr-ma-shēn″), ''n.'' In ''shoemaking'', any one of the various machines used in cutting out or shaping the uppers of boots and shoes, including ''crimping-'', ''trimming-'', and ''seaming-machines''.

'''uppermost''' (up′ėr-mōst), ''a. superl.'' [< ''upper'' + ''most''; cf. ''upmost''.] '''1.''' Highest in place; first in precedence: as, the ''uppermost'' seats.
{{smaller block|Euen vpon the ''uppermost'' pinnacle of the temple.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Luke iv.}}}}
'''2.''' Highest in power; predominant; most powerful; first in force or strength.
{{smaller block|Whatever faction happens to be ''uppermost''. {{right|''Swift.''}}
<poem>As in perfumes composed with art and cost,
’Tis hard to say what scent is ''uppermost''.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Eleanora, l. 154.}}}}

'''uppermost''' (up′ėr-mōst), ''adv. superl.'' '''1.''' In the highest position or place; also, first in a series or in order of time.
{{smaller block|They [the primitive Quakers] committed to writing whatever words came ''uppermost'', as fast as the pen could put them down, and subjected to no after-revision what had been produced with no forethought.
{{right|''Southey'', Life of Bunyan, p. 41.}}}}
'''2†.''' First in order of precedence.
{{smaller block|All Dukes daughters shall goe all-one with a nother, soe that alwayes the Eldest Dukes Daughter go ''vpermost''.
{{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 14.}}}}

'''upper-stocks†''' (up′ėr-stoks), ''n. pl.'' Breeches. Also ''overstocks''. Compare ''nether-stock''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy ''upper-stockes'', be they stuft with silk or flocks,
Never become thee like a nether pair of stocks.</poem>
{{right|''J. Heywood'', Epigrams. (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''uppertendom''' (up-ėr-ten′dum), ''n.'' [< ''upper ten'' + ''-dom.''] Same as ''upper ten thousand'' (which see, under ''upper'').

'''up-pile''' (up-pīl′), ''v. t.'' To pile up; heap up. ''Southey'', Thalaba, ii. [Rare.]

'''upping''' (up′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of *''up'', ''v.'', < ''up'', ''adv.''] The act of marking a swan on the upper mandible. See ''swan-upping''.

'''uppish''' (up′ish), ''a.'' [< ''up'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Proud; arrogant; airy; self-assertive; assuming. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|It seems daring to rail at informers, projectors, and officers was not ''uppish'' enough, but his Lordship must rise so high as daring to limit the power and revenue of the Crown. {{right|''Roger North'', Examen, p. 48. (''Davies.'')}}
Half-pay officers at the parade very ''uppish'' upon the death of the King of Spain.
{{right|''Tom Brown'', Works, I. 154. (''Davies.'')}}
Americans are too ''uppish;'' but when you get hold of a man that is accustomed to being downtrodden, it ’s easy to keep him so. {{right|''F. R. Stockton'', Merry Chanter, xvii.}}}}
'''2.''' Tipsy. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|''Lady Head.'' Not so drunk, I hope, but that he can drive us?
''Serv.'' Yes, yes, Madam, he drives best when he ’s a little ''upish.'' {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Journey to London, iii. 1.}}}}

'''uppishly''' (up′ish-li), ''adv.'' In an uppish manner.

'''uppishness''' (up′ish-nes), ''n.'' The character of being uppish; arrogance; airiness; pretentiousness; self-assertion.
{{smaller block|I sometimes question whether that quality in him [Landor] which we cannot but recognize and admire, his loftiness of mind, should not sometimes rather be called ''uppishness'', so often is the one caricatured into the other by a blusterous self-confidence and self-assertion.
{{right|''Lowell'', The Century, XXXV. 512.}}}}

'''up-plight†''', ''v. t.'' [ME., < ''up'' + ''plight''<sup>3</sup>.] To fold up; carry off.
{{smaller block|The gates of the toun he hath ''upplyght.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 59.}}}}

'''up-pluck''' (up-pluk′), ''v. t.'' To pluck up; pull up. [Rare.]

'''up-prop''' (up-prop′), ''v. t.'' To prop up; sustain by a prop. ''Donne'', Progress of the Soul, i.

'''up-putting''' (up′pu̇t″ing), ''n.'' Lodging; entertainment for man and beast. ''Scott.'' [Scotch.]

'''upraise''' (up-rāz′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''upreysen''; < ''up'' + ''raise''<sup>1</sup>.] To raise; lift up.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon a night

'''upraising''' (up′rā″zing), ''n.'' Rearing; nurture. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There was nothing of the Corydon about Hunt or his ''upraising'', as the Scotch call it.
{{right|''The Portfolio'', N. S., No. 13, p. 10.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
